title: A helyedben...: Giving Advice by Imagining Yourself in Their Place

sections.title: Standing where someone else stands
sections.content: Hungarian has a compact, very natural way to give advice: instead of telling someone what to do, you say what you would do if you were standing in their place. *hely* ("place, spot") takes a possessive ending for whose place it is, plus *-ben* ("in"): *helyedben* literally means "in your place". Pair it with a conditional-mood verb — but conjugated for the ADVICE-GIVER, usually *én* ("I") — and you get a classic piece of Hungarian advice: *A helyedben (én) szólnék a főnöknek*, "In your place, I'd talk to the boss."

sections.title: The advice-giver speaks, in the conditional

items.spanish: A helyedben én szólnék a főnökömnek.
items.english: In your place, I'd talk to my boss.

items.spanish: Az ő helyében sokkal óvatosabb lennék.
items.english: In his/her place, I'd be much more careful.
In your place (you all), I'd leave right now.

sections.content: This is the trap: *helyedben* already means "in YOUR place", so it's tempting to also put the verb in the *te*-form. Don't — the verb stays in whoever is doing the imagining, almost always *én*: *A helyedben én mennék*, not *A helyedben te mennél*. The person being advised only appears once, inside *helyedben* itself.
